intro:
Al-Fātiḥah is the chapter that opens the Book. Its name means "The Opening," and it carries that name for two reasons: the Book of Allah begins with it, and every unit of prayer begins with it as well. No prayer is complete without it, which is why the scholars call it the key to the whole Qur'an.

Most of the early authorities place its revelation in Makkah. Ibn Kathir records that Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah and Abū al-ʿĀliyah all held that view, and the majority of the scholars followed them. Al-Alūsī preserves the one voice on the other side: Mujāhid said it came down in Madinah, and the scholars who came after him counted that as a slip. The practical argument settles the question. The five prayers were made obligatory in Makkah, and the prayer is not valid without this chapter. The Muslims must therefore have had it in their hands before they left Makkah.

The chapter has several names, and each one describes a different job it does. Ibn Kathir lists them from the early reports. It is al-Fātiḥah, the Opener. It is Umm al-Kitāb and Umm al-Qurʾān, the Mother of the Book and the Mother of the Qur'an, because everything in the Book is gathered in it. It is al-Sabʿ al-Mathānī, the Seven Oft-Repeated Verses, a name the Qur'an gives it directly: (15:87 — *“We have certainly granted you the seven often-repeated verses and the great Quran”*). It is also called al-Hamd and al-Ṣalāh, because it is praise from beginning to end and because the prayer is named after it. Two more names describe what it does for a reader: al-Shifāʾ, the Cure, and al-Ruqyah, the healing recitation.

The scholars counted its letters with care. Ibn Kathir reports that the chapter holds twenty-five words and one hundred and thirteen letters. Al-Qurṭubī gave it twenty-seven separate questions in his commentary, because so many rulings and meanings sit inside those few lines. Al-Bukhārī explained the mother-name in the simplest way: the Qur'an starts with it, and the prayer starts by reciting it. Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī added the Arabic behind the name. The Arabs call any matter that gathers many parts an umm. They call the skin around the brain umm ar-raʾs, and the banner that gathers the army an umm, and Makkah Umm al-Qurā because it leads the settlements.

Its rank in the Book is described in the hadith. At-Tirmidhī, who graded the report ṣaḥīḥ, records Abū Hurayrah hearing the Prophet ﷺ call it the Mother of the Qur'an, the Mother of the Book, the seven repeated verses and the glorious Qur'an. Aḥmad records Abū Saʿīd ibn al-Muʿallā being told he would be taught the greatest sūrah in the Qur'an, and discovering that it was this one. Aḥmad also records Ubayy ibn Kaʿb being told that nothing like it had been sent down in the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms or the Qur'an; At-Tirmidhī received the same report and graded it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ. Muslim and An-Nasāʾī record Ibn ʿAbbās describing a door in heaven opened for this Prophet ﷺ alone, from which an angel brought two lights no prophet had been given before: the Opening of the Book and the closing verses of Sūrah al-Baqarah. Its use as a healing recitation is in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, where Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī treated a stung tribal chief with it and the Prophet ﷺ asked him how he knew it was a healing recitation, then told the group to divide the sheep they had been paid and give him a share.

Two rulings keep the chapter in a Muslim's life every day. Muslim records Abū Hurayrah reporting that the Prophet ﷺ said three times that whoever prays without Umm al-Qur'an has prayed incompletely. When Abū Hurayrah was asked what a person standing behind the imam should do, he answered that such a person should recite it quietly, and he quoted the ḥadīth qudsī behind the ruling: "I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves, and My servant shall have what he asks for." The two Ṣaḥīḥs record ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit reporting the same requirement in a harder form, "There is no prayer for whoever does not recite the Opening of the Book."

The chapter has one clear turn. Verses 1:1 to 1:4 speak about God: His Name, His praise, His mercy, His mastery of the Day of Judgement. Verse 1:5 turns and speaks to Him. The last two verses are requests that God Himself taught the servant to make. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes that the middle verse holds both halves at once, because "You alone we worship" is praise and "You alone we ask for help" is a request. The ḥadīth qudsī in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim describes the chapter as divided into two halves between Allah and His servant, and the dividing line falls exactly at that verse. The whole chapter is spoken in the plural, so the one praying speaks for every believer. Maudūdī's Tazkir al-Qurʾān sums it up: this chapter is Islam in miniature, and the rest of the Qur'an is the enlargement of that picture.

verses.1:
> In the Name of Allah—the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful

**“In the Name of Allah”**

This line is called the basmalah. It stands at the head of one hundred and thirteen chapters of the Qur'an. Only Sūrah al-Tawbah opens without it. Inside the text of the Qur'an it appears one other time, in the letter the Prophet Sulaymān sent to the Queen of Sheba: (27:30 — *“It is from Solomon, and it reads: ‘In the Name of Allah—the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful”*).

The first word of revelation ever brought to the Prophet ﷺ carried the same instruction: (96:1 — *“Read, ˹O Prophet,˺ in the Name of your Lord”*). The Muslim begins with the Name of Allah because the Qur'an begins there, and because God is the one who makes every act possible. Al-Ṭabarī explains the line as the servant's announcement that he starts with the Name of his Lord, seeking His help and His blessing in what he is about to do.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān makes the point concrete. Before Islam, the Arabs began their journeys, their deals and their poems with the names of their idols. Islam replaced that habit at the root. When the Prophet ﷺ first began his mission, he would open an act with the words *Bismika Allāhumma*, "In Your name, O Allah." When this full line was revealed, he adopted it and taught it to his community. So the words on our tongues today are the answer to a very old habit.

Think of a man who must cross a wide river. He can step into the boat and trust his own arms, or he can begin by naming the One who made the water, the wood and the strength in his own shoulders. The basmalah is that moment of turning before the first stroke.

**“the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful”**

The two names come from one root, *raḥmah*, which means mercy. Al-Mukhtaṣar explains that both names describe the same mercy, and that they tell the reader how wide it is: it surrounds everything and reaches every living being, and the believers receive the largest share of it. Al-Saʿdī puts it in the old form: the mercy of Allah covers every creature, and it is completed for the people who follow the messengers He sent.

The order carries a lesson. The line does not open with the Mighty, the Judge or the Avenger. It opens with mercy, and it opens with mercy twice. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the Qur'an keeps fear and hope together on purpose. A servant who knows how great Allah is may despair; a servant who hears only about mercy may grow careless. The basmalah teaches both from the first breath: the One you are standing before is great, and the One you are standing before is kind.

Al-Saʿdī adds a point of belief. These are not decorative titles. They tell us that mercy is a real attribute of Allah, and that everything good in the world flows from it, the way light flows from the sun.
verses.2:
> All praise is for Allah—Lord of all worlds

**“All praise is for Allah”**

Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī explains the sentence as a declaration that every kind of thanks belongs to Allah alone. It does not belong to any idol, and it does not belong to any creature. He then lists some of the favours behind the thanks: the body that carries out the commands of Allah, the food that keeps the body alive, the guidance that shows a person where to walk. The favours cannot be counted, and the ability to thank Him is itself one of them.

Ibn Kathir preserves a report from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb. He once asked ʿAlī about this phrase. The community already knew what "there is no god but Allah" meant, and "glory be to Allah", and "Allah is greatest"; what did *al-ḥamdu lillāh* add? ʿAlī answered that it is a statement Allah loved for Himself and was pleased with for Himself, and that He likes to hear it repeated. Ibn ʿAbbās, in a report recorded by Ibn Abī Ḥātim, said that when the servant says these words, Allah answers, "My servant has praised Me."

The definite article carries weight. Ibn Kathir explains that the *al* at the front of *al-ḥamd* gathers every kind of praise. The sentence does not claim one thank-you for Allah. It hands Him all of them.

**“Lord of all worlds”**

Rabb means owner and master, the one with full authority over what he holds. It also carries a second sense, the one who raises a thing step by step until it reaches its purpose. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes that the word belongs to Allah alone, and that a person can only use it for someone else with a qualifier attached, as in "the master of the house."

Al-ʿālamīn is the plural of ʿālam, and it means everything other than Allah. Ibn Kathir collects the opinions of the early scholars on how wide that is. Al-Farrāʾ and Abū ʿUbayd limited it to beings with minds: the jinn, humankind, the angels and the devils, not the animals. Zayd ibn Aslam and Abū Muḥaysin included everything created with a soul. Qatādah said that every kind of creature is an ʿālam. Al-Qurṭubī concluded that the word covers everything Allah created in this world and the next. The verse is short, and it places the one who recites it inside a creation too large to count.

The Qur'an shows what this lordship means in practice. When Pharaoh asked Moses who this "Lord of all worlds" was, the answer was plain: (26:24 — *“˹He is˺ the Lord of the heavens and the earth and everything in between, if only you had sure faith.”*).

Maudūdī, in Tazkir al-Qurʾān, draws out why the praise belongs to one Owner. Think of a garden with many streams. Every stream looks separate, and each one waters its own bed. Follow them all back, and the water comes from a single spring. Praise works the same way. When a person admires a flower, a poem, a cure or a kindness, he is admiring something made. Trace it back and it ends at the One who made it.
verses.3:
> the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful

**“the Most Compassionate”**

Al-Raḥmān names the mercy of Allah that reaches everything. Al-Mukhtaṣar explains that the name comes from *raḥmah*, mercy, and that its purpose here is to show how vast that mercy is: it surrounds the whole of creation and embraces every living thing. Al-Saʿdī says the same in the language of the early scholars: the mercy of Allah is wide enough to cover every creature He made.

The Qur'an states the breadth in one short line: (7:156 — *“But My mercy encompasses everything”*). The commentators drew a careful distinction from this name and the one that follows it. Al-Raḥmān is mercy toward creation as such, without looking at what a person has done. Al-Raḥīm is the mercy that carries a believer all the way to the end.

The two names appear here, right after "Lord of all worlds," and al-Qurṭubī explains the order. Lordship over every world puts awe in the heart. The two mercy names put hope back. He cites the Qur'anic pair that keeps the two feelings together, and the verse that follows it seals the pairing: (15:49 — *“Inform My servants ˹O Prophet˺ that I am truly the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”*), and then (15:50 — *“and that My torment is indeed the most painful”*). He supports the same point with a report in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim from Abū Hurayrah: if a believer knew the full extent of Allah's punishment, nobody would hope for Paradise, and if an unbeliever knew the full extent of His mercy, nobody would despair of it.

Al-Jalālayn defines mercy in a way a child can follow: mercy is wanting what is good for the one who needs it.

**“Most Merciful”**

The second name, al-Raḥīm, turns mercy into a relationship. It travels with the servant and works on his case. The Qur'an says of the Prophet ﷺ that he came as mercy for the world: (21:107 — *“We have sent you ˹O Prophet˺ only as a mercy for the whole world”*). It gives the same assurance to anyone who has wandered far: (39:53 — *“O My servants who have exceeded the limits against their souls! Do not lose hope in Allah’s mercy, for Allah certainly forgives all sins.”*). Muḥammad Shafīʿ, writing in Maʿārif al-Qurʾān, notes that the name is often joined to the mention of the Hereafter for this reason: it is the mercy that keeps a believer going until he arrives.

Al-Saʿdī makes a point here that protects belief. These two names are not slogans. They tell us that Allah has a real attribute of mercy, that every blessing in the world is a trace of it, and that a hardened heart is not caused by any shortage on His side.

Imagine standing in the rain. The rain falls on the field of the farmer who prepared his soil, and it falls on the rock beside the road, on the good man's roof and on the thief's. That is how the mercy of al-Raḥmān arrives. Now picture the same rain soaked into the fields and turned into a harvest. That is al-Raḥīm: mercy that reaches its purpose in the life of a believer.
verses.4:
> Master of the Day of Judgment

**“Master of the Day of Judgment”**

The word here is read in two ways, and both readings come down from the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Bayḍāwī records that ʿĀṣim, al-Kisāʾī and Yaʿqūb read *mālik*, "owner," while the rest of the reciters read *malik*, "king." He notes that the scholars of the two sacred cities chose the second reading. The two words are not rivals. An owner disposes of what he owns as he wishes. A king commands and forbids those under him. The verse names the Day on which both belong to one Lord without a partner.

**Why That Day Is Named**

Allah is Master of every day. Why single out this one? Ibn Kathir answers that on that Day the ownership of everyone else comes to an end. Nobody will claim anything. Nobody will speak without permission. The Qur'an paints that silence more than once. On that Day the spirit and the angels will stand in ranks and none will talk except the one whom the Most Compassionate allows: (78:38 — *“on the Day the ˹holy˺ spirit and the angels will stand in ranks. None will talk, except those granted permission by the Most Compassionate”*). The Prophet ﷺ described the same hush in words the two Ṣaḥīḥs record: (20:108 — *“All voices will be hushed before the Most Compassionate”*). Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk reports from Ibn ʿAbbās the plain meaning of the verse: on that Day nobody owns what he used to own in the world.

The Qur'an puts the question of the Day into a single announcement: (40:16 — *“Who does all authority belong to this Day? To Allah—the One, the Supreme”*). The two Ṣaḥīḥs record the Prophet ﷺ describing the scene that goes with it. Allah will grasp the earth, fold the heavens in His right hand and call out, "I am the King. Where are the kings of the earth? Where are the tyrants? Where are the arrogant?"

**What Recompense Means**

*Dīn* here means the settling of accounts. Ibn Kathir supports the meaning from the Qur'an's own use of the word, where it describes a full payment of what is due: (24:25 — *“On that Day, Allah will give them their just penalty in full”*). Maʿārif al-Qurʾān adds a second argument, from fairness. The world is the field of action, not the hall of payment. A rich man may be far from God, and a sick man may be close to Him. If no account were ever settled, the courtroom of justice would stand empty. The Qur'an asks the question twice to wake the reader up: (82:17 — *“What will make you realize what Judgment Day is”*), and then again at (82:18 — *“Again, what will make you realize what Judgment Day is”*).

ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, in a saying Ibn Kathir records, left the community a rule for daily life: hold yourselves accountable before you are held accountable, and weigh your deeds before they are weighed. The two Ṣaḥīḥs also record a warning about titles: the most despised name before Allah belongs to a man who calls himself king of kings, because no owner exists except Allah.

Think of a marketplace. All year the traders buy and sell, and nobody is stopped at the gate. Then one morning the gates close for the final audit. Every account book is opened in order, and every deal is read aloud. The verse tells the reader that such a morning is coming, and that the Master of that market is the One being addressed here.
verses.5:
> You ˹alone˺ we worship and You ˹alone˺ we ask for help

**“You ˹alone˺ we worship”**

Until this verse the chapter speaks about God. Here it begins to speak to Him. Al-Qurṭubī notes the change and describes what it does: the worshipper moves from praise into intimate address in a single step. Al-Bayḍāwī reads the same movement as a walk from proof to sight, so that what the servant knew about his Lord he now says to His face. The classical commentators draw one practical lesson from it. No priest stands between the worshipper and God. Every believer is invited to speak this line himself.

Arabic allows a sentence to be built in more than one order, and this verse puts the object first. Al-Zamakhsharī explains the placement as a device of exclusivity: the meaning is that worship is for You alone and for nobody else. Al-Qurṭubī records how naturally the Arabs used that order. A man insulted another and the second man turned away. The first said, "You are the one I mean." The second answered, "And it is you I turn away from."

Worship here is more than ritual. Al-Ṭabarī reports that the community agreed that the root of the word lies in humility and submission. The same root describes a path that feet have trodden until it is smooth, which is why the word serves both for a road and for a servant. The confession "You alone we worship" therefore says three things at once: You are my Owner, I am Your servant, and I obey You.

Al-Ṭabarī also preserves a report from the early Sufi teachers through Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq: worship comes in three kinds. Some people worship God out of fear, and that is the worship of slaves. Some worship Him hoping for reward, and that is the worship of hired workers. Some worship Him out of love, and that is the worship of free people, and that is the best of the three.

**“and You ˹alone˺ we ask for help”**

Worship is mentioned before the request, and the scholars explain why. A man does not ask a king for help before he has greeted the king and accepted him as king. Picture a worker who walks into a large workshop on his first morning. Before he asks the foreman for tools, he puts himself under the foreman's orders and learns the rules of the house. Only then does he ask, and the tools come. Al-Ṭabarī defines the second half of the verse as the servant asking his Lord for help in worshipping Him, in obeying Him, and in every matter of his life, from no one besides Him. He records a report from Ibn ʿAbbās with exactly that sense, and he is honest about the chain: he grades it weak, and says so.

The Qur'an explains why this help is needed every hour of the day: (47:38 — *“For Allah is the Self-Sufficient, whereas you stand in need ˹of Him˺”*). It also names the two tools that carry a person through: (2:45 — *“And seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, it is a burden except for the humble”*). And it gives the reason the request is answered at all: (40:60 — *“Call upon Me, I will respond to you”*).

Muslim records the ḥadīth qudsī in which this verse is the hinge of the chapter. Allah says that the prayer is divided between Him and His servant, and that when the servant reaches these words, He answers, "This is between Me and My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks for." Everything before this verse was the servant's praise. Everything after it is his petition.
verses.6:
> Guide us along the Straight Path

**“Guide us”**

Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, quoted at length in Maʿārif al-Qurʾān, defines guidance as leading someone toward his destination gently and kindly, and he notes that in its fullest sense guidance comes from Allah alone. He describes it in degrees. The first degree is shared by everything created, because every creature was given its nature and then directed to what that nature needs. The Qur'an says it plainly: (20:50 — *“Our Lord is the One Who has given everything its ˹distinctive˺ form, then guided ˹it˺”*). The guidance asked for in this verse is a higher kind: the leading of a person who can choose, toward what pleases God.

The request raises an obvious question. The one praying already believes. Why ask for guidance again, every day, in every prayer? Ibn Kathir gives the answer that the servant needs his Lord every hour, both to stay firm and to move forward. The Qur'an commands believers to believe, a command that only makes sense as a call to steadiness: (4:136 — *“O believers! Have faith in Allah, His Messenger, the Book He has revealed to His Messenger, and the Scriptures He revealed before”*). It also teaches the prayer that protects what has already been given: (3:8 — *“Our Lord! Do not let our hearts deviate after you have guided us”*).

There is a second question inside the request. God has already shown every human being two roads: (90:10 — *“and shown them the two ways ˹of right and wrong˺”*). Knowing the road exists is not the same as walking it. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān compares guidance to the work of a guide in strange country. A traveller may hold a map, and still need someone who knows the land to walk beside him.

**“along the Straight Path”**

Al-Ṭabarī reports that the community agreed on the meaning of *ṣirāṭ mustaqīm*: a clear road with no branches. He supports it with a line of poetry from Jarīr ibn ʿAṭiyyah, who described a leader standing on a road that stays straight while other roads bend. He then notes how the Arabs used the same picture for conduct, calling an honest man straight and a dishonest man crooked, and he concludes that the road the Qur'an names is Islam.

Ibn Kathir records the prophetic picture of that road. Aḥmad records in his Musnad the report of an-Nawwās ibn Samʿān, that the Prophet ﷺ described a straight path with two walls on either side, doors standing open in the walls, and curtains hanging over the doors. A caller at the mouth of the path called out, "O people, enter the path and keep straight." Another caller above the path warned anyone reaching for a door, "Do not open it, for if you open it you will pass through." The Prophet ﷺ then named every part of the picture. The path is Islam. The two walls are the limits Allah set. The open doors are what He has forbidden. The caller at the path is the Book of Allah, and the caller above it is the warning Allah places in the heart of every Muslim.

The Qur'an describes the same road from the other end, asking which of two travellers is better off: (67:22 — *“Who is ˹rightly˺ guided: the one who crawls facedown or the one who walks upright on the Straight Path”*). And it gives the road a name that a reader can carry: (6:153 — *“Indeed, that is My Path—perfectly straight. So follow it and do not follow other ways, for they will lead you away from His Way.”*)
verses.7:
> the Path of those You have blessed—not those You are displeased with, or those who are astray

**“the Path of those You have blessed”**

Verse 1:6 asked for a road. This verse names the road by the people who walk it. The Qur'an gives the roster in one line: (4:69 — *“And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger will be in the company of those blessed by Allah: the prophets, the people of truth, the martyrs, and the righteous—what honourable company”*). Four ranks, one shared description. Every one of them received favour from God, and none of them earned it by right.

Al-Ṭabarī collects the early attempts to identify these people. Ibn ʿAbbās listed the angels, the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous, in a report whose chain al-Ṭabarī himself grades weak. Rabīʿ ibn Anas said they are the prophets. Wakīʿ said they are the believers, and Ibn Jurayj heard from Ibn ʿAbbās that they are the believers as well. Al-Ṭabarī prefers the wider reading, and his reason comes from the text itself: the verse describes people whom God has favoured, and the favour is not limited to one rank.

Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Bayḍāwī both stop at the grammar, and their point is worth having. The phrase "the path of those You have blessed" stands in apposition to "the Straight Path," which means the verse does not just add a description. It defines the road. The straight path is, by God's own naming, the road the blessed ones walked. That gives a reader a way to test any claim to be on the right road: look at where the footprints lead.

**“not those You are displeased with”**

The first failure named here is the failure of a person who knew the truth and turned away from it. Al-Jalālayn and al-Mukhtaṣar both read the phrase that way, and al-Mukhtaṣar ties it to the Israelites, who had the covenant in front of them and did not carry it. The classical identification behind the phrase is the Jews, but the description is wider than one nation.

Ibn Kathir records the report in Aḥmad's Musnad in which ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim heard the Prophet ﷺ explain both groups, and he also keeps the picture honest. Both descriptions, he says, apply to both communities. He cites the Qur'an for each emphasis: (5:60 — *“It is those who earned Allah’s condemnation and displeasure”*) describes people who were cursed and made targets of wrath, while (5:77 — *“nor follow the vain desires of those who went astray before ˹you˺”*) describes people who wandered and led others to wander.

**“or those who are astray”**

The second failure is softer and more common. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes it as the failure of a person who did not seek the truth in the first place, and ties the description to the Christians, whose mistake lay in the search rather than in the knowledge. Ibn Kathir records the same division through the Prophet's ﷺ words to ʿAdī, and he notes how often the Qur'an uses the word "astray" for this condition: (4:136 — *“whoever denies Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and the Last Day has clearly gone far astray”*).

Two failures, then, and two ways of missing the same road. One traveller studies the timetable, memorises the route, and refuses to board the train. The other never looks at the timetable at all and wanders the platform. The verse asks the reader to belong to neither group, and to walk with the blessed.

The chapter closes with a word that asks God to make all of this true. Muslim records that when the servant recites these last verses, Allah answers, "This is for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks for." Ibn Kathir explains the closing *Āmīn* as the servant's request that his prayer be accepted, and At-Tirmidhī glossed it as a plea not to be let down in hope. Ibn Kathir collects the evidence for saying it. Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd and At-Tirmidhī record Wāʾil ibn Ḥujr hearing the Prophet ﷺ recite the end of the chapter and then say *Āmīn*, lengthening his voice, and At-Tirmidhī graded the report ḥasan. The two Ṣaḥīḥs record the Prophet ﷺ saying that when the imam says *Āmīn* the people should say it, because whoever's *Āmīn* falls together with the *Āmīn* of the angels has his past sins forgiven.
